newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Ex-paramilitary troops take Guatemalan refinery.
newsitem.headline: Ex-paramilitary troops take Guatemalan refinery.

text.p: Some 700 former paramilitary soldiers took over an oil refinery in the northern Guatemala jungle and threatened to burn it down if the government did not agree to pay them for wartime service, national police and oil company officials said on Friday.
"They say they are ready to die," Guatemalan National Guard spokesman Faustino Sanchez said.
Two hundred guardsmen were sent to the Basic Petroleum International refinery in the Peten jungle on Friday to reinforce police and army troops stationed in the area, Sanchez said.

Members of the region's now-defunct civil defence patrols -- paramilitary groups organised and armed by the military during the previous decade -- are demanding $10,000 each. It was their second attack in two weeks against Basic, Guatemala's sole oil producer and refiner.

Work stopped when the action began on Thursday, and all employees except five technicians were evacuated from the refinery, located about 140 miles (225 km) from Guatemala City, said company spokesman Luis de Leon.

The plant processes 20,000 barrels of crude oil a day for the export market, and the stoppage represents a loss of $200,000 daily, De Leon said. Basic is owned by investors from the United States, France and Canada, he said.

The former paramilitary soldiers, some accompanied by their wives, demanded a meeting with President Alvaro Arzu on Friday. On Thursday they attempted to take the nearby Santa Elena airport but failed, Sanchez said.
The patrols, dissolved under the Dec. 29 peace accords, were born of the government's counterinsurgency campaign of the 1980s. Service often was obligatory in communities under military control.
The units were blamed for some of the worst human rights abuses of Guatemala's 36-year civil war, in which an estimated 100,000 died and 40,000 disappeared.
